item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q007_chey_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places these domains in distinct families of the CheY-like superfamily (c.23.1), within the flavodoxin-like fold (c.23) and α/β class: CheY-related response regulators (c.23.1.1), the ornithine-decarboxylase N-terminal wing (c.23.1.2), and the KaiA N-terminal domain (c.23.1.3). This superfamily-level assignment supports remote common ancestry and conservation of a CheY-like structural core; it is stronger than mere fold similarity but does not make the families functionally interchangeable. It does not show that the ODC wing or KaiA N-terminal domain accepts phosphate on a receiver Asp, participates in a histidine-kinase phosphorelay, or produces a CheY-like signaling output. Conversely, it does not imply that CheY proteins or KaiA decarboxylate ornithine, bind PLP, or contain the ODC catalytic site; the wing is only one domain of the larger enzyme. Nor does it transfer KaiA-specific circadian/KaiC regulation to CheY or ODC, or establish that the KaiA N-terminal domain itself has canonical receiver chemistry. A member of one family may template the shared core, but it is not a functional representative for the whole superfamily: phosphorylation assays and phosphoacceptor-residue evidence, PLP/enzyme assays and active-site evidence, or KaiC-binding/clock assays are respectively required before making those claims.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
